title: حِكَايَةُ عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ مَعَ شَمْسِ النَّهَارِ
titleEn: ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār
part: Night 164 · ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 795–798 (Night 164, continuing directly from nights-163), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 164 continues the tale of ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār. The jeweller, ruined and mocked after the raid on his house, is fetched by a stranger who leads him by night across the river to a locked house, where ten men — the thieves — give him food and drink and ask his story. They have ʿAlī and Shams al-Nahār, and have not touched them for their dignity. Trusting them, the jeweller tells everything; the thieves, dismayed to learn who their captives are, apologise and promise to return his goods. They take the three back across the river, but horsemen of the watch surround them on the bank; the thieves escape by boat. The jeweller's story that they are singers does not convince the horsemen, until Shams al-Nahār speaks privately with their captain, who mounts her on his own horse and sees all three home by boat. At nightfall ʿAlī falls into a swoon, and his household turn to the jeweller for an explanation. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الرَّابِعَةُ وَالسِّتُّونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-rābiʿatu wa-al-sittūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the fourth-and-sixty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and sixty-fourth night,
sentences.n: The heading is built as before: al-rābiʿa, “the fourth”, feminine to agree with layla; then wa-al-sittūn, “and the sixty”; then baʿda al-miʾa, “after the hundred”.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الْجَوْهَرِيَّ لَمَّا سَمِعَ الْكَلَامَ رَجَعَ إِلَى دَارِهِ الثَّانِيَةِ الَّتِي هُوَ سَاكِنٌ بِهَا وَقَالَ فِي نَفْسِهِ إِنَّ الَّذِي حَصَلَ لِي هُوَ الَّذِى خَافَ مِنْهُ أَبُوالْحَسَنِ وَذَهَبَ إِلَى الْبَصْرَةِ وَقَدْ وَقَعْتُ فِيهِ أَنَا
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-jawhariyya lammā samiʿa al-kalāma rajaʿa ilā dārihi al-thāniyati allatī huwa sākinun bihā wa-qāla fī nafsihi inna alladhī ḥaṣala lī huwa alladhī khāfa minhu Abū al-Ḥasani wa-dhahaba ilā al-Baṣrati wa-qad waqaʿtu fīhi anā
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the jeweller, when he heard the speech, returned to his-house, the second, which he (is) dwelling in-it, and said within-himself: That-which has-befallen me (is) that-which Abū al-Ḥasan feared (from-it) and went to Basra; and I have fallen into-it, I (myself).
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that when the jeweller heard these words he went back to his other house, the one he lived in, and said to himself, “What has befallen me is the very thing Abū al-Ḥasan feared when he went off to Basra; and now I have fallen into it myself.”
sentences.n: The night takes up again the sentence that closed the last one: the jeweller's return to “his second house, the one he lives in” (see the note there on al-thāniya, “the other”). fī nafsihi, “within himself”, introduces thought, not speech. Inside it the narration slips from “he” to “I”, into the jeweller's own voice. alladhī khāfa minhu, “that which he feared”: khāfa takes min for the thing feared, and the -hu points back to alladhī. Abū al-Ḥasan is the perfumer who first carried the lovers' messages and then left for Basra, fearing just this. waqaʿtu fīhi anā: the added anā stresses the subject, “I myself”; the damma of وقعتُ is the print's own. The print sets Abū al-Ḥasan as one word, ابوالحسن, and spells alladhī the second time with ى.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ نَهْبَ دَارِةِ اشْتَهَرَ عِنْدَ النَّاسِ فَأَقْبَلَ إِلَيْهِ النَّاسُ مِنْ كُلِّ جَانِبٍ وَمَكَانٍ فَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ هُوَ شَامِتٌ بِهِ وَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ هُوَ عَاذِرٌ وَحَامِلٌ هَمَّهُ
sentences.tr: thumma inna nahba dārihi ishtahara ʿinda al-nāsi fa-aqbala ilayhi al-nāsu min kulli jānibin wa-makānin fa-minhum man huwa shāmitun bihi wa-minhum man huwa ʿādhirun wa-ḥāmilun hammahu
sentences.l: Then (indeed) the plundering of his-house became-known among the people, and the people came-forward to-him from every side and place; and of-them (was) who he (was) gloating over-him, and of-them who he (was) excusing (him) and bearing his-care.
sentences.i: Then the looting of his house became common talk, and people came to him from every side and quarter: some of them gloating over him, others making allowances for him and sharing his trouble.
sentences.n: dārihi, “his house”, is printed دارة: the print often writes the pronoun -hu with tā' marbūṭa; it is read as the pronoun. The narration is back in the third person. thumma inna, “then (indeed)”, is a common narrative opener, not real emphasis. man huwa shāmitun bihi, “one who was gloating over him”: shamita bi- is to rejoice at another's misfortune. ʿādhir, “excusing”, one who holds him blameless; ḥāmilun hammahu, “carrying his care”, sharing his distress. The shadda of همّه is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَصَارَ يَشْكُولَهُمْ وَلَمْ يَأْكُلْ طَعَامًا وَلَمْ يَشْرَبْ شَرَابًا مِمَّابِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-ṣāra yashkū lahum wa-lam yaʾkul ṭaʿāman wa-lam yashrab sharāban mimmā bihi
sentences.l: And he-took-to complaining to-them, and he-ate not food and drank not drink, from-what (was) in-him.
sentences.i: He took to pouring out his complaints to them, and for all that weighed on him he would neither eat nor drink.
sentences.n: The print runs two pairs of words together: يشكولهم for yashkū lahum, “he complains to them”, and ممابه for mimmā bihi, “from what was in him”, i.e. from grief; each is kept as one word and pointed within. ṣāra with an imperfect, “he took to, began”. mā bihi, “what is in him”, is the usual idiom for a man's distress or sickness. ṭaʿāman … sharāban, each verb with its own noun: “ate no food, drank no drink”. yaʾkul has its hamza in the print.

sentences.t: فَبَيْنَمَا هُوَ جَالِسٌ مُتَنَدِّمٌ وَإِذَا بِغُلَامٍ مِنْ غِلْمَانِهِ دَخَلَ عَلَيْهِ وَقَالَ لَهُ إِنَّ شَخْصًا بِالْبَابِ يَدْعُوكَ لَمْ أَعْرِفْهُ
sentences.tr: fa-baynamā huwa jālisun mutanaddimun wa-idhā bi-ghulāmin min ghilmānihi dakhala ʿalayhi wa-qāla lahu inna shakhṣan bi-al-bābi yadʿūka lam aʿrifhu
sentences.l: And while he (was) sitting regretful, and behold, a-lad of his-lads came-in upon-him and said to-him: A-figure (is) at-the-door calling-you; I-did- not -know-him.
sentences.i: As he sat there, full of regret, one of his servant lads came in to him and said, “There is someone at the door asking for you, a man I do not know.”
sentences.n: baynamā … wa-idhā, “while … behold”, is the Nights' usual frame for an interruption; bi- after idhā only marks what appears. mutanaddim, Form V of nadima, “regretful, full of remorse”, stands beside jālis as a second circumstantial word. shakhṣ, “a figure, someone”, a person not yet named. lam aʿrifhu, “I do not know him (lit. I did not know him)”, is added with no linking word.

sentences.t: فَخَرَجَ الْجَوْهَرِيُّ إِلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ عَلَيْهِ وَوَجَدَهُ إِنْسَانًا لَمْ يَعْرِفْهُ
sentences.tr: fa-kharaja al-jawhariyyu ilayhi wa-sallama ʿalayhi wa-wajadahu insānan lam yaʿrifhu
sentences.l: So the jeweller went-out to-him and greeted him, and found-him a-person he-did- not -know-him.
sentences.i: The jeweller went out to him and greeted him, and found him to be a man he did not know.
sentences.n: wajada with two objects, “to find someone (to be) something”. lam yaʿrifhu describes insānan; because that noun is indefinite, the describing clause needs no relative pronoun. The shadda of سلّم is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الرَّجُلُ إِنَّ لِي حَدِيثًا بَيْنِي وَبَيْنَكَ فَأَدْخَلَهُ الدَّارَ وَقَالَ لَهُ مَاعِنْدَكَ مِنَ الْحَدِيثِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-rajulu inna lī ḥadīthan baynī wa-baynaka fa-adkhalahu al-dāra wa-qāla lahu mā ʿindaka mina al-ḥadīthi
sentences.l: And the man said to-him: I-have a-talk between-me and between-you. So he-brought-him-into the house and said to-him: What (is) with-you of talk?
sentences.i: The man said to him, “I have something to say to you in private.” So the jeweller took him into the house and said to him, “What is it you have to tell me?”
sentences.n: inna lī ḥadīthan, “I have a matter to tell”: li- marks the possessor. baynī wa-baynaka, “between me and you”, i.e. for us two alone; Arabic repeats bayna with each pronoun. The print runs ما عندك together as ماعندك. mina al-ḥadīth, “of talk”: min names the kind of thing asked about.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الرَّجُلُ امْضِ مَعِي إِلَى دَارِكَ الثَّانِيَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-rajulu imḍi maʿī ilā dārika al-thāniyati
sentences.l: And the man said to-him: Go with-me to your-house, the second.
sentences.i: The man said to him, “Come with me to your other house.”
sentences.n: Here al-thāniya is the jeweller's second house in the plain sense: the one he fitted out for the lovers, which the thieves have stripped.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْجَوْهَرِيُّ وَهَلْ تَعْرِفُ دَارِي الثَّانِيَةَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-jawhariyyu wa-hal taʿrifu dārī al-thāniyata
sentences.l: And the jeweller said: And do you-know my-house, the second?
sentences.i: “So you know my other house?” said the jeweller.
sentences.n: wa-hal, “and do …?”: the wa- gives the question a note of surprise, much like English “So you know …?”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ إِنَّ جَمِيعَ خَبَرِكَ عِنْدِي وَإِنَّ عِنْدِي أَيْضًا مَايُفَرِّجُ اللَّهُ بِهِ هَمَّكَ عَنْكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla inna jamīʿa khabarika ʿindī wa-inna ʿindī ayḍan mā yufarriju Allāhu bihi hammaka ʿanka
sentences.l: And he-said: Indeed all your-story (is) with-me, and indeed with-me also (is) what God will-relieve by-it your-care from-you.
sentences.i: He said, “I know your whole story, and I have besides that by which God will lift your trouble from you.”
sentences.n: farraja hamman ʿan, “to lift care from someone”. mā yufarriju Allāhu bihi, “that by which God will relieve”: bihi points back to mā. The print runs ما يفرج together as مايفرج; the shadda of همّك is its own.

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ فِي نَفْسِى أَنَا أَمْضِي مَعَهُ حَيْثُ أَرَادَ ثُمَّ تَوَجَّهْتُ إِلَى أَنْ أَتَيْنَا الدَّارَ
sentences.tr: fa-qultu fī nafsī anā amḍī maʿahu ḥaythu arāda thumma tawajjahtu ilā an ataynā al-dāra
sentences.l: So I-said within-myself: I, I-will-go with-him where he-wished. Then I-set-out, until we-came-to the house.
sentences.i: I said to myself, “I will go with him wherever he likes.” Then I set out, and at length we reached the house.
sentences.n: The narration is in the first person again: the jeweller tells his own story. anā amḍī, with the pronoun set first, “as for me, I will go”, a resolve. ilā an with the perfect, “until (in fact) we came”. The print spells nafsī with ى.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّارَأَى الرَّجُلُ الدَّارَ قَالَ إِنَّهَا بِغَيْرِ بَابٍ وَلَابَوَّابٍ وَلَا يُمْكِنُ الْقُعُودُ فِيهَا فَامْضِ بِنَا إِلَى غَيْرِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾā al-rajulu al-dāra qāla innahā bi-ghayri bābin wa-lā bawwābin wa-lā yumkinu al-quʿūdu fīhā fa-imḍi binā ilā ghayrihā
sentences.l: And when the man saw the house, he-said: It (is) without door and no doorkeeper, and not possible (is) the sitting in-it; so go with-us to other-than-it.
sentences.i: When the man saw the house he said, “It has neither door nor doorkeeper, and there is no sitting in it. Let us go somewhere else.”
sentences.n: The print runs together فلما رأى as فلمارأى and ولا بواب as ولابواب. The second is read wa-lā bawwābin, “and no doorkeeper”, which pairs naturally with bāb, “door”: the thieves had carried off even the doors. The same letters could be read wa-lā abwābin, “and no doors”, but that only repeats bāb. bi-ghayri, “with other than”, i.e. “without”. imḍi binā, “go with us”, i.e. “take us, let us be off”: bi- of company.

sentences.t: فَلَمْ يَزَلِ الرَّجُلُ يَدُورُ مِنْ مَكَانٍ إِلَى مَكَانٍ وَأَنَا مَعَهُ حَتَّى دَخَلَ عَلَيْنَا اللَّيْلُ وَلَمْ أَسْأَلْهُ عَنْ أَمْرٍ مِنَ الْأُمُورِ
sentences.tr: fa-lam yazali al-rajulu yadūru min makānin ilā makānin wa-anā maʿahu ḥattā dakhala ʿalaynā al-laylu wa-lam asʾalhu ʿan amrin mina al-umūri
sentences.l: And the man did- not -cease going-round from place to place, and I (was) with-him, until the night came-in upon-us; and I-did- not -ask-him about a-matter of the matters.
sentences.i: The man went on wandering from place to place, and I with him, until night came down upon us; and I asked him nothing at all.
sentences.n: lam yazal with an imperfect, “he did not cease (doing)”, i.e. “he kept on”. dakhala ʿalaynā al-layl, “night came in upon us”: nightfall. ʿan amrin mina al-umūr, “about a matter of the matters”, i.e. about anything at all. The middle hamza of asʾalhu is printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُ لَمْ يَزَلْ يَمْشِي وَأَنَا أَمْشِي مَعَهُ حَتَّى خَرَجْنَا إِلَى الْفَضَاءِ وَهُوَ يَقُولُ اتَّبِعْنِي
sentences.tr: thumma innahu lam yazal yamshī wa-anā amshī maʿahu ḥattā kharajnā ilā al-faḍāʾi wa-huwa yaqūlu ittabiʿnī
sentences.l: Then he did- not -cease walking, and I walking with-him, until we-went-out to the open-space, he saying: Follow-me.
sentences.i: Then he kept on walking, and I walking with him, until we came out into the open country, and all the while he kept saying, “Follow me.”
sentences.n: al-faḍāʾ, “the open space”, the empty ground beyond the houses. wa-huwa yaqūlu, “he saying”, a circumstantial clause: what went on as they walked. ittabiʿnī, Form VIII imperative of tabiʿa, “follow me”.

sentences.t: وَصَارَ يُهَرْوِلُ فِي مَشْيِهِ وَأَنَا أُهَرْوِلُ وَرَاءَةُ وَأُقَوِّي قَلْبِي عَلَى الْمَشْيِ حَتَّى أَتَيْنَا الْبَحْرَ
sentences.tr: wa-ṣāra yuharwilu fī mashyihi wa-anā uharwilu warāʾahu wa-uqawwī qalbī ʿalā al-mashyi ḥattā ataynā al-baḥra
sentences.l: And he-took-to trotting in his-walking, and I trotting behind-him and strengthening my-heart for the walking, until we-came-to the river.
sentences.i: He broke into a jog as he went, and I jogged along behind him, steeling myself to keep going, until we came to the river.
sentences.n: harwala, “to trot, go at a jog”, between a walk and a run; the print points it both times (يُهَرْول, اُهَرْوِل), and those marks are its own. warāʾahu, “behind him”, is printed وراءة, the pronoun again written with tā' marbūṭa. qawwā qalbahu ʿalā, “to strengthen one's heart for”, to nerve oneself to. al-baḥr is literally “the sea”, but the word is used of any great river; here it is the Tigris.

sentences.t: فَطَلَعَ بِنَا فِى زَوْرَقٍ وَقَذَفَ بِنَا الْمَلَّاحُ حَتَّى عَدَّانَا إِلَى الْبَرِّ الثَّانِي
sentences.tr: fa-ṭalaʿa binā fī zawraqin wa-qadhafa binā al-mallāḥu ḥattā ʿaddānā ilā al-barri al-thānī
sentences.l: And he-went-up with-us into a-skiff, and the boatman rowed with-us until he-took-us-across to the shore, the second.
sentences.i: He took us aboard a skiff, and the boatman rowed us on until he had brought us over to the far bank.
sentences.n: The print has الناني, a misprint for الثاني, corrected here. al-barr al-thānī, “the second shore”, is the far bank. ṭalaʿa binā fī zawraqin, “he went up with us into a skiff”, i.e. took us aboard: bi- makes the verb carry someone along. qadhafa, “to throw”, is in boatmen's use “to row” (miqdhāf, an oar); qadhafa binā, “rowed with us (aboard)”. ʿaddā, Form II of ʿadā, “to take across”, a word of everyday speech: ʿaddānā, “he ferried us over”.

sentences.t: فَنَزَلَ مِنْ ذَٰلِكَ الزَّوْرَقِ وَنَزَلْتُ خَلْفَهُ فَأَخَذَ الرَّجُلُ بِيَدِى وَنَزَلَ بِي فِي دَرْبٍ لَمْ أَدْخُلْهُ طُولَ عُمْرِى وَلَمْ أَعْلَمْ هُوَ فِي أَيِّ نَاحِيَةٍ
sentences.tr: fa-nazala min dhālika al-zawraqi wa-nazaltu khalfahu fa-akhadha al-rajulu bi-yadī wa-nazala bī fī darbin lam adkhulhu ṭūla ʿumrī wa-lam aʿlam huwa fī ayyi nāḥiyatin
sentences.l: And he-got-down from that skiff, and I-got-down behind-him; and the man took (me) by-my-hand, and went-down with-me into a-lane I-had- not -entered-it the length of my-life, and I-did- not -know (in) which quarter it (was).
sentences.i: He stepped out of the skiff and I after him. Then the man took me by the hand and led me down into a lane I had never entered in all my life, and I did not know what quarter of the city it was in.
sentences.n: nazala min, “to get down from”, of leaving a boat. akhadha bi-yadī, “took (me) by my hand”: bi- marks the part taken hold of. nazala bī, “went down with me”, i.e. led me down; bi- again carries the narrator along. ṭūla ʿumrī, “the length of my life”, an adverbial accusative: “ever in my life”. wa-lam aʿlam huwa fī ayyi nāḥiyatin, “nor did I know in what quarter it was”: an indirect question set down with no linking word. The print writes yadī and ʿumrī with ى; the shadda of أيّ is its own.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الرَّجُلَ وَقَفَ عَلَى بَابِ دَارٍ وَفَتَحَهَا وَدَخَلَ وَأَدْخَلَنِي مَعَهُ وَأَغْلَقَ بَابَهَا بِقُفْلٍ مِنْ حَدِيدٍ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-rajula waqafa ʿalā bābi dārin wa-fataḥahā wa-dakhala wa-adkhalanī maʿahu wa-aghlaqa bābahā bi-quflin min ḥadīdin
sentences.l: Then the man stood at the door of a-house, and opened-it, and went-in, and brought-me-in with-him, and locked its-door with a-lock of iron.
sentences.i: Then the man stopped at the door of a house, opened it, went in and took me in with him, and locked the door behind us with an iron lock.
sentences.n: waqafa ʿalā bābi dārin, “stopped at the door of a house”: ʿalā is “at, by”. fataḥahā, “opened it”: -hā is the house (dār is feminine), though it is the door that opens. min ḥadīd, “of iron”: min of material.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ مَشَي بِي فِي دِهْلِيزِهَا حَتَّى دَخَلْنَا عَلَى عَشَرَةِ رِجَالٍ كَأَنَّهُمْ رَجُلٌ وَاحِدٌ هُمْ إِخْوَانٌ
sentences.tr: thumma mashā bī fī dihlīzihā ḥattā dakhalnā ʿalā ʿasharati rijālin ka-annahum rajulun wāḥidun hum ikhwānun
sentences.l: Then he-walked with-me in its-entrance-passage until we-entered upon ten men as-though-they (were) one man; they (were) brothers.
sentences.i: Then he led me along its entrance passage until we came in upon ten men, so alike that they might have been one man: they were brothers.
sentences.n: mashā bī, “he walked with me”, i.e. led me. The print spells mashā with a dotted ي (مشي) where Classical spelling has ى; it is read mashā all the same. dihlīz, “vestibule, entrance passage”, a Persian loan; its -hā refers back to the house. dakhala ʿalā, “to go in to (someone)”. ʿasharatu rijālin: with the numbers three to ten the numeral takes the opposite gender to its noun, so masculine rijāl has feminine ʿashara. ka-annahum, “as though they (were)”.

sentences.t: قَالَ الْجَوْهَرِيُّ فَسَلَّمْنَا عَلَيْهِمْ فَرَدُّوا عَلَيْنَا السَّلَامَ وَأَمَرُونَا بِالْجُلُوسِ فَجَلَسْنَا
sentences.tr: qāla al-jawhariyyu fa-sallamnā ʿalayhim fa-raddū ʿalaynā al-salāma wa-amarūnā bi-al-julūsi fa-jalasnā
sentences.l: The jeweller said: So we-greeted them, and they-returned to-us the greeting, and ordered-us to sitting, so we-sat.
sentences.i: The jeweller said: We greeted them, and they returned our greeting and bade us sit, and we sat down.
sentences.n: The narrator's frame slips in again mid-story: “the jeweller said”. amara bi-, “to command (something)”: the bi- marks the thing commanded, here al-julūs, “sitting”. The shadda of ردّوا is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَكُنْتُ قَدْ هَلَكْتُ مِنْ شِدَّةِ التَّعَبِ فَجَاؤُا إِلَيَّ بِمَاءِ وَرْدٍ وَرَشُّوهُ عَلَى وَجْهِي وَسَقَوْنِي شَرَابًا وَقَدَّمُوا إِلَيَّ طَعَامًا وَأَكَلَ بَعْضُهُمْ مَعِي
sentences.tr: wa-kuntu qad halaktu min shiddati al-taʿabi fa-jāʾū ilayya bi-māʾi wardin wa-rashshūhu ʿalā wajhī wa-saqawnī sharāban wa-qaddamū ilayya ṭaʿāman wa-akala baʿḍuhum maʿī
sentences.l: And I-had already perished from the-severity of-the-weariness; so they-came to-me with water of-rose and sprinkled-it on my-face, and gave-me-to-drink a-drink, and set-before me food, and some-of-them ate with-me.
sentences.i: I was all but dead with weariness, so they brought me rose-water and sprinkled it on my face, gave me something to drink, and set food before me, and some of them ate with me.
sentences.n: kuntu qad halaktu, “I had perished”, an overstatement for “I was worn out to death”. jāʾa bi-, “to bring” (literally “to come with”). The print spells jāʾū as جاؤا, with the hamza on wāw and no second wāw; this is an old spelling of جاءوا. māʾ ward, “rose-water”, a genitive phrase. saqā, “to give to drink”, takes two objects: saqawnī sharāban, “they gave me a drink”. The shaddas of اليّ and رشّوه are the print's own.

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ لَوْكَانَ فِى الطَّعَامِ شَيْءٌ مُضِرٌّ لَمْ يَأْكُلُوا مِنْهُ مَعِي
sentences.tr: fa-qultu law kāna fī al-ṭaʿāmi shayʾun muḍirrun lam yaʾkulū minhu maʿī
sentences.l: So I-said: If there-were in the-food a-thing harmful, they-would- not -have-eaten from-it with-me.
sentences.i: I said to myself, “If there were anything harmful in the food, they would not have eaten it with me.”
sentences.n: The print has فقات, a misprint for فقلت, corrected here. The “saying” is inward: the jeweller reasons with himself. law … lam yaʾkulū, “if … they would not have eaten”: a negative answer to law takes lam with the jussive, as here, or mā with the perfect; nothing loose about it. The print runs law and kāna together (لوكان) and spells fī with ى; both are kept. The shadda of مضرّ is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا غَسَلْنَا أَيْدِيَنَا عَادَ كُلٌّ مِنَّا إِلَى مَكَانِهِ وَقَالُوا هَلْ تَعْرِفُنَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā ghasalnā aydiyanā ʿāda kullun minnā ilā makānihi wa-qālū hal taʿrifunā
sentences.l: And when we-washed our-hands, each of-us returned to his-place, and they-said: Do you-know-us?
sentences.i: When we had washed our hands, each of us went back to his place, and they said, “Do you know us?”
sentences.n: Hands were washed after eating as well as before. kullun minnā, “each one of us”, with tanwīn standing for the omitted noun.

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ لَا وَلَا عُمْرِي رَأَيْتُكُمْ بَلْ وَلَا رَأَيْتُ الَّذِي أَحْضَرَنِي إِلَيْكُمْ وَلَا رَأَيْتُ هَذَا الْمَوْضِعَ أَبَدًا
sentences.tr: fa-qultu lā wa-lā ʿumrī raʾaytukum bal wa-lā raʾaytu alladhī aḥḍaranī ilaykum wa-lā raʾaytu hādhā al-mawḍiʿa abadan
sentences.l: So I-said: No, and not (in) my-lifetime have-I-seen-you; nay, and not did-I-see the-one-who brought-me to-you, and not did-I-see this place ever.
sentences.i: I said, “No; never in my life have I seen you. Nor, for that matter, have I ever seen the man who brought me to you, or this place, before.”
sentences.n: lā ʿumrī, “never in my life”, literally “not (in) my lifetime”, a colloquial turn: ʿumrī stands as an adverb and the lā negates the perfect raʾaytukum. bal wa-lā, “nay, nor even”. aḥḍara, Form IV, “to bring, cause to be present”. The second raʾaytu is printed without its hamza (رايت), the first and third with it (رأيت); all three are the same word.

sentences.t: فَقَالُوا أَطْلِعْنَا عَلَى خَبَرِكَ وَلَا تَكْذِبْ فِي شَيْءٍ
sentences.tr: fa-qālū aṭliʿnā ʿalā khabarika wa-lā takdhib fī shayʾin
sentences.l: So they-said: Make-us-acquainted with your-story, and do- not -lie in anything.
sentences.i: They said, “Tell us your story, and do not lie in anything.”
sentences.n: aṭliʿnā, imperative of Form IV aṭlaʿa ʿalā, “to let (someone) see, inform (someone) of”, with the object suffix -nā, “us”. lā takdhib, the jussive after lā of prohibition.

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ لَهُمُ اعْلَمُوا أَنَّ حَالِي عَجِيبٌ وَأَمْرِى غَرِيبٌ فَهَلْ عِنْدَكُمْ شَيْءٌ مِنْ خَبَرِي
sentences.tr: fa-qultu lahumu iʿlamū anna ḥālī ʿajībun wa-amrī gharībun fa-hal ʿindakum shayʾun min khabarī
sentences.l: So I-said to-them: Know that my-state (is) wondrous and my-affair strange; so is there with-you anything of my-news?
sentences.i: I said to them, “Know that my case is a wondrous one and my affair a strange one. Do you know anything of what has happened to me?”
sentences.n: ʿajīb and gharīb rhyme, a touch of sajʿ in the jeweller's speech. The print spells amrī with ى (وامرى); it is read with -ī all the same. The question is pointed: the jeweller suspects these men have something to do with what befell him.

sentences.t: قَالُوا نَعَمْ نَحْنُ الَّذِي أَخَذْنَا أَمْتِعَتَكَ فِى اللَّيْلَةِ الْمَاضِيَةِ وَأَخَذْنَا صَدِيقَكَ وَالَّتِي كَانَتْ تُغَنِّي مَعَهُ
sentences.tr: qālū naʿam naḥnu alladhī akhadhnā amtiʿataka fī al-laylati al-māḍiyati wa-akhadhnā ṣadīqaka wa-allatī kānat tughannī maʿahu
sentences.l: They-said: Yes; we (are) the-one-who took your-goods in the-night the-past, and we-took your-friend and the-one-who was singing with-him.
sentences.i: They said, “Yes. It was we who took your goods last night, and we took your friend too, and the woman who was singing with him.”
sentences.n: naḥnu alladhī: the singular relative alladhī stands for the plural alladhīna, as often in Middle Arabic, and the verb that follows agrees with naḥnu: “we who took”. amtiʿa, plural of matāʿ, “goods, household stuff”. fī al-laylati al-māḍiyati, “in the past night”, i.e. last night. The shadda of تغنّي is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ لَهُمْ أَسْبَلَ اللَّهُ عَلَيْكُمْ سِتْرَهُ أَيْنَ صَدِيقِي هُوَ وَالَّتِي كَانَتْ تُغَنِّي مَعَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-qultu lahum asbala Allāhu ʿalaykum sitrahu ayna ṣadīqī huwa wa-allatī kānat tughannī maʿahu
sentences.l: So I-said to-them: May-God-let-down upon-you His-veil! Where (is) my-friend, he and the-one-who was singing with-him?
sentences.i: I said to them, “May God let His covering veil fall over you! Where is my friend, and the woman who was singing with him?”
sentences.n: asbala Allāhu ʿalaykum sitrahu, a perfect used as a wish: “may God let down His veil over you”, i.e. keep your faults hidden and you safe from disgrace; a courteous blessing to soften the question. ayna ṣadīqī huwa, “where is my friend, he”: the pronoun huwa resumes ṣadīqī so that the second subject can be joined to it.

sentences.t: فَأَشَارُوا إِلَيَّ بِأَيْدِيهِمْ إِلَى نَاحِيَةٍ وَقَالُوا هُهُنَا
sentences.tr: fa-ashārū ilayya bi-aydīhim ilā nāḥiyatin wa-qālū huhunā
sentences.l: So they-pointed to-me with-their-hands toward a-side, and they-said: Here.
sentences.i: They pointed with their hands toward one side of the house, and said, “In there.”
sentences.n: ashāra ilā, “to make a sign to (someone)”; here ilayya is the one signed to and ilā nāḥiyatin the direction pointed. nāḥiya, “side, quarter”. The print sets “here” as هُهنا with a damma on the first letter, a form of hāhunā (ها هنا), “here”; the print's damma is kept and the word is pointed huhunā to match it. The shadda of اليّ is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَلَكِنْ وَاللَّهِ يَا أَخِي مَا ظَهَرَ سِرُّهُمَا عَلَى أَحَدٍ مِنَّا غَيْرَكَ
sentences.tr: wa-lākin wa-Allāhi yā akhī mā ẓahara sirruhumā ʿalā aḥadin minnā ghayraka
sentences.l: But by-God, O my-brother, their-secret has- not -appeared to anyone of-us other-than-you.
sentences.i: “But by God, my brother, their secret has not come out to any one of us; you are the only one who knows it.
sentences.n: ẓahara ʿalā, “to become apparent to, come to the knowledge of”. ghayraka, “other than you, except you”, in the accusative of exception. The thieves do not know who the pair are; only the jeweller does. The shadda of سرّهما is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَمِنْ حِينِ أَتَيْنَا بِهِمَا لَمْ نَرَهُمَا إِلَى هَذَا الْوَقْتِ وَلَمْ نَسْأَلْهُمَا عَنْ حَالِهِمَا لِمَا رَأَيْنَا عَلَيْهِمَا مِنَ الْهَيْبَةِ وَالْوَقَارِ
sentences.tr: wa-min ḥīni ataynā bihimā lam narahumā ilā hādhā al-waqti wa-lam nasʾalhumā ʿan ḥālihimā li-mā raʾaynā ʿalayhimā mina al-haybati wa-al-waqāri
sentences.l: And from (the) time we-brought them, we-have- not -seen-them until this time, and we-have- not -asked-them about their-state, because-of what we-saw upon-them of awe and dignity.
sentences.i: From the moment we brought them here until now we have not looked in on them, nor asked them who they are, because of the awe and dignity we saw in them.
sentences.n: atā bi-, “to bring” (literally “to come with”). lam narahumā, jussive of raʾā, “we have not seen them”, i.e. have not gone in to them. li-mā, “because of what”; min introduces what that was: al-hayba, “awe, the majesty that inspires fear”, and al-waqār, “gravity, dignity”.

sentences.t: وَهَذَا هُوَ الَّذِي مَنَعَنَا عَنْ قَتْلِهِمَا
sentences.tr: wa-hādhā huwa alladhī manaʿanā ʿan qatlihimā
sentences.l: And this (is) it which prevented-us from killing-them.
sentences.i: And that is what has kept us from killing them.
sentences.n: huwa, a pronoun of separation between subject and predicate: “this is the thing that …”. manaʿa ʿan, “to prevent from”; manaʿanā, “it prevented us” (not manaʿnā, “we prevented”).

sentences.t: فَأَخْبِرْنَا عَنْ حَقِيقَةِ أَمْرِهِمَا وَأَنْتَ فِى أَمَانٍ عَلَى نَفْسِكَ وَعَلَيْهِمَا
sentences.tr: fa-akhbirnā ʿan ḥaqīqati amrihimā wa-anta fī amānin ʿalā nafsika wa-ʿalayhimā
sentences.l: So inform-us about the truth of their-affair, and you (are) in safety upon your-self and upon-the-two-of-them.
sentences.i: So tell us the truth about these two; you are safe, both you and they.”
sentences.n: akhbirnā, imperative of akhbara (Form IV), “inform us”, with ʿan for the matter told. wa-anta fī amānin, a circumstantial clause, “while you are under safe-conduct”: amān is the pledge of safety given to someone who might fear harm. ʿalā nafsika wa-ʿalayhimā, “for your own life and theirs”. The print writes fī with alif maqṣūra (فى).

sentences.t: قَالَ الْجَوْهَرِيُّ فَلَمَّا سَمِعْتُ هَذَا الْكَلَامَ كِدْتُ أَنْ أَهْلِكَ مِنَ الْخَوْفِ وَالْفَزَعِ
sentences.tr: qāla al-jawhariyyu fa-lammā samiʿtu hādhā al-kalāma kidtu an ahlika mina al-khawfi wa-al-fazaʿi
sentences.l: The jeweller said: And when I-heard this speech, I-almost (did) that I-perish from the fear and the terror.
sentences.i: The jeweller said: When I heard these words I all but died of fear and terror.
sentences.n: kidtu, “I was on the point of”, from kāda; Classical usage prefers the bare imperfect after it (kidtu ahliku), but kāda an … with the subjunctive is common, and is what the print has. halaka, “to perish”.

sentences.t: وَقُلْتُ لَهُمْ يَا إِخْوَانِي اعْلَمُوا أَنَّ الْمُرُوَّةَ إِذَا ضَاعَتْ لَمْ تُوجَدْ إِلَّا عِنْدَكُمْ
sentences.tr: wa-qultu lahum yā ikhwānī iʿlamū anna al-muruwwata idhā ḍāʿat lam tūjad illā ʿindakum
sentences.l: And I-said to-them: O my-brothers, know that manliness, when it-is-lost, it-is- not -found except with-you.
sentences.i: I said to them, “My brothers, know that if true chivalry were lost everywhere else, it would still be found among you.
sentences.n: muruwwa, “manliness, chivalry”, the code of honour and generosity of a man of standing; the Classical spelling is with hamza (muruʾa), and the print's مروة is the usual softened form, read muruwwa. lam tūjad, passive jussive of wajada, “it is not found”: after idhā the past is general, “whenever it is lost”. The shadda of الّا is the print's own. The jeweller is flattering the thieves for his life.

sentences.t: وَإِذَا كَانَ عِنْدِي سِرٌّأَخَافُ إِنْشَاءَهُ فَلَا يُخْفِيهِ إِلَّا صُدُورُكُمْ
sentences.tr: wa-idhā kāna ʿindī sirrun akhāfu inshāʾahu fa-lā yukhfīhi illā ṣudūrukum
sentences.l: And when there-is with-me a-secret (whose) spreading I-fear, nothing hides-it except your-breasts.
sentences.i: And if I have a secret that I dread to see spread abroad, none but your breasts can keep it hidden.”
sentences.n: The print runs sirrun and akhāfu together as one word (سرّاخاف); the spacing is kept and the two words are read. The shadda is the print's own. akhāfu inshāʾahu is an adjective clause on an indefinite noun, with no relative word: “a secret whose spreading I fear”. inshāʾ normally means “bringing into being, composing”; the sense wanted is plainly “divulging”, ifshāʾ (افشاء), which differs from the print by the shape of one letter, so the print may be at fault. Since inshāʾ might perhaps be stretched to “setting (a story) going”, and the reading is not certain, the print's word is kept and read inshāʾ. The hamza on the line (ء) is the print's own. ṣudūr, “breasts”, the seat of kept secrets.

sentences.t: وَصِرْتُ أُبَالِغُ لَهُمْ فِي هَذَا الْمَعْنَى
sentences.tr: wa-ṣirtu ubālighu lahum fī hādhā al-maʿnā
sentences.l: And I-set-about going-to-lengths to-them in this meaning.
sentences.i: And I went on at length to them in this vein.
sentences.n: ṣāra with an imperfect, “to begin to, set about”. bālagha fī (Form III), “to go to great lengths in, exaggerate”. al-maʿnā, “the meaning”, here “the theme, this line of talk”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنِّي وَجَدْتُ الْمُبَادَرَةَ لَهُمْ بِالْحَدِيثِ أَنْفَعَ وَأَحْسَنَ مِنْ كِتْمَانِهِ
sentences.tr: thumma innī wajadtu al-mubādarata lahum bi-al-ḥadīthi anfaʿa wa-aḥsana min kitmānihi
sentences.l: Then I found the hastening to-them with the story more-useful and better than concealing-it.
sentences.i: Then I judged that to tell them the story straight out would serve me better and be wiser than to hide it.
sentences.n: wajada with two accusatives, “to find (something) to be (so)”: al-mubādarata … anfaʿa wa-aḥsana. bādara (Form III), “to hasten, be beforehand”; bādarahu bi-, “to come out with something to someone without delay”, so bi- marks what is told. anfaʿ and aḥsan are elatives, “more useful”, “better”, with min for “than”. kitmān, verbal noun of katama, “to keep secret”.

sentences.t: فَحَدَّثْتُهُمْ بِجَمِيعِ مَا وَقَعَ لِي حَتَّى انْتَهَيْتُ إِلَى آخِرِ الْحَدِيثِ
sentences.tr: fa-ḥaddathtuhum bi-jamīʿi mā waqaʿa lī ḥattā intahaytu ilā ākhiri al-ḥadīthi
sentences.l: So I-told-them of all what befell to-me, until I-reached to the end of the story.
sentences.i: So I told them all that had befallen me, from first to last.
sentences.n: ḥaddatha bi-, “to tell (someone) of”: the person told is the object, the matter takes bi-. waqaʿa li-, “to happen to”. intahā ilā, “to come to (the end)”. The madda of آخر is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعُوا حِكَايَتِي قَالُوا وَهَلْ هَذَا الْفَتَى عَلِيُّ بْنُ بَكَّارٍ وَهَذِهِ الْجَارِيَةُ شَمْسُ النَّهَارِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿū ḥikāyatī qālū wa-hal hādhā al-fatā ʿAliyyu ibnu Bakkārin wa-hādhihi al-jāriyatu Shamsu al-Nahāri
sentences.l: And when they-heard my-tale, they-said: And is this young-man ʿAlī son of Bakkār, and this girl Shams al-Nahār?
sentences.i: When they had heard my tale, they said, “Then is this young man ʿAlī ibn Bakkār, and this girl Shams al-Nahār?”
sentences.n: hal asks a plain yes-or-no question; the wa- before it is a touch of surprise, “why, is this …?” Each half is a nominal sentence with no verb “to be”: hādhā al-fatā, “this young man”, is the subject, ʿAliyyu ibnu Bakkārin the predicate. Shams al-Nahār, “Sun of the Day”.

sentences.t: قُلْتُ نَعَمْ
sentences.tr: qultu naʿam
sentences.l: I-said: Yes.

sentences.t: فَصَعُبَ عَلَيْهِمْ ذَلِكَ وَقَامُوا وَاعْتَذَرُوا لَهُمَا
sentences.tr: fa-ṣaʿuba ʿalayhim dhālika wa-qāmū wa-iʿtadharū lahumā
sentences.l: And that was-hard upon-them, and they-rose and excused-themselves to-the-two.
sentences.i: That weighed heavily on them; they rose and begged the pair's pardon.
sentences.n: ṣaʿuba ʿalā, “to be hard on, grieve”. iʿtadhara li- (Form VIII), “to make one's excuses to, apologise to”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالُوا لِي إِنَّ الَّذِي أَخَذْنَاهُ مِنْ دَارِكَ ذَهَبَ بَعْضُهُ وَهَذَا بَاقِيهِ
sentences.tr: thumma qālū lī inna alladhī akhadhnāhu min dārika dhahaba baʿḍuhu wa-hādhā bāqīhi
sentences.l: Then they-said to-me: That-which we-took-it from your-house, some-of-it has-gone, and this (is) the-rest-of-it.
sentences.i: Then they said to me, “Of what we took from your house, part is gone; here is the rest.”
sentences.n: alladhī akhadhnāhu, “what we took”: the -hu on the verb points back to alladhī, as Arabic relative clauses require. The whole phrase is the subject of inna, and its predicate is a sentence of its own, dhahaba baʿḍuhu, “part of it has gone”. bāqīhi, “its remainder”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ رَدُّوا إِلَيَّ أَكْثَرَ الْأَمْتِعَةِ وَالْتَزَمُوا أَنَّهُمْ يُعِيدُونَهَا إِلَى مَحَلِّهَا فِي دَارِي وَيَرُدُّونَ لِي الْبَاقِيَ
sentences.tr: thumma raddū ilayya akthara al-amtiʿati wa-iltazamū annahum yuʿīdūnahā ilā maḥallihā fī dārī wa-yaruddūna lī al-bāqiya
sentences.l: Then they-returned to-me most-of the goods, and bound-themselves that they would-bring-them-back to their-place in my-house, and give-back to-me the rest.
sentences.i: Then they gave me back most of the goods, and undertook to carry them back to their places in my house and to restore the rest to me as well.
sentences.n: akthar, “more, most”, before a definite plural means “most of”: akthara al-amtiʿati, “most of the goods”. iltazama (Form VIII), “to bind oneself, undertake”, here with anna and a clause. yuʿīdūnahā, Form IV of ʿāda, “to bring back”. The two clauses seem to tell it twice, once as done and once as promised: they handed over most of the goods there and then, and undertook to carry them home and make good what was missing. The shaddas of ردّوا and اليّ are the print's own.

sentences.t: فَاطْمَأَنَّ قَلْبِي وَلَكِنَّهُمُ انْقَسَمُوا نِصْفَيْنِ فَصَارَ قِسْمٌ مِنْهُمْ مَعِي وَقِسْمٌ مِنْهُمْ عَلَيَّ
sentences.tr: fa-iṭmaʾanna qalbī wa-lākinnahumu inqasamū niṣfayni fa-ṣāra qismun minhum maʿī wa-qismun minhum ʿalayya
sentences.l: And my-heart was-at-rest; but they divided-themselves (in) two-halves, and a-part of-them came-to-be with-me and a-part of-them against-me.
sentences.i: My heart grew easier; but they split into two halves, one half on my side and the other against me.
sentences.n: iṭmaʾanna, “to be at rest, reassured”; its hamza is the print's own. lākinnahum takes a helping u before the next word's joining alif: lākinnahumu inqasamū. inqasama (Form VII), “to be divided, split”. maʿī … ʿalayya, “with me … against me”: maʿa and ʿalā are the usual pair for taking a side, so some of the band took his part and some did not, which is what the lākin, “but”, after his relief prepares for. The print's shadda on عليّ marks ʿalayya, “against me”; ʿAlī (ʿAliyy, also written عليّ) can hardly be meant, since the name would want maʿa, “with”, before it.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ خَرَجْنَا مِنْ تِلْكَ الدَّارِ
sentences.tr: thumma kharajnā min tilka al-dāri
sentences.l: Then we-went-out from that house.
sentences.i: Then we left that house.

sentences.t: هَذَا مَا كَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِي وَأَمَّا مَا كَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِ عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ وَشَمْسِ النَّهَارِ فَإِنَّهُمَا قَدْ أَشْرَفَا عَلَى الْهَلَاكِ مِنْ شِدَّةِ الْخَوْفِ
sentences.tr: hādhā mā kāna min amrī wa-ammā mā kāna min amri ʿAliyyi ibni Bakkārin wa-Shamsi al-Nahāri fa-innahumā qad ashrafā ʿalā al-halāki min shiddati al-khawfi
sentences.l: This (is) what was of my-affair. And as-for what was of the affair of ʿAlī son of Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār, they-two had come-near upon destruction from the severity of the fear.
sentences.i: So much for me. As for ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār, they were at death's door from sheer terror.
sentences.n: hādhā mā kāna min amrī … wa-ammā mā kāna min amri …, “this is what happened with me … and as for what happened with …”, the storyteller's stock way of turning from one thread to another, though here the jeweller uses it within his own tale. ammā … fa-, “as for … (then)”. ashrafa ʿalā, “to overlook from a height”, hence “to be on the verge of”: ashrafā ʿalā al-halāki, “they were on the brink of perishing”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنِّي تَقَدَّمْتُ إِلَى عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ وَشَمْسِ النَّهَارِ وَسَلَّمْتُ عَلَيْهِمَا
sentences.tr: thumma innī taqaddamtu ilā ʿAliyyi ibni Bakkārin wa-Shamsi al-Nahāri wa-sallamtu ʿalayhimā
sentences.l: Then I stepped-forward to ʿAlī son of Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār and greeted them-two.
sentences.i: Then I went up to ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār and greeted them.
sentences.n: thumma innī, “then I”: the emphatic inna is often used in the Nights simply to carry a pronoun at the head of a clause. sallama ʿalā, “to greet”.

sentences.t: وَقُلْتُ لَهُمَا يَاتُرَى كَيْفَ جَرَى بِالْجَارِيَةِ وَالْوَصِيفَتَيْنِ وَأَيْنَ ذَهَبْنَ
sentences.tr: wa-qultu lahumā yā turā kayfa jarā bi-al-jāriyati wa-al-waṣīfatayni wa-ayna dhahabna
sentences.l: And I-said to-them-two: O, is-it-seen, how went (it) with the slave-girl and the two-maids, and where did-they(f.)-go?
sentences.i: And I said to them, “What, I wonder, has become of the slave-girl and the two maids? Where have they gone?”
sentences.n: yā turā, literally “O, is it seen?”, a stock phrase for “I wonder”, printed as one word (ياترى); the spacing is kept. jarā bi-, “to befall, happen to”: kayfa jarā bi-al-jāriyati, “how did it go with the slave-girl?” waṣīfa, “maid, girl in service”; waṣīfatayni is its dual. dhahabna, “they went”, feminine plural.

sentences.t: فَقَالَا لَاعِلْمَ لَنَا بِهِنَّ
sentences.tr: fa-qālā lā ʿilma lanā bihinna
sentences.l: And the-two said: No knowledge to-us of-them(f.).
sentences.i: They said, “We know nothing of them.”
sentences.n: The print runs lā and ʿilm together (لاعلم); the spacing is kept. lā ʿilma, the lā that denies a whole class, “there is no knowledge”; lanā, “to us”, marks who has (or lacks) it, and bi- marks what is known: ʿilm bi-, “knowledge of”.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ نَزَلْ سَائِرِينَ إِلَي أَنِ انْتَهَيْنَا إِلَي الْمَكَانِ الَّذِي فِيهِ السُّمَيْرِيَّةُ
sentences.tr: wa-lam nazal sāʾirīna ilā an intahaynā ilā al-makāni alladhī fīhi al-sumayriyyatu
sentences.l: And we-did- not -cease going until that we-came to the place which in-it (was) the sumayriyya.
sentences.i: And we kept on walking until we came to the place where the boat was moored.
sentences.n: lam nazal, “we did not cease”, with the participle sāʾirīna in the accusative as its predicate: “we kept going”. The “we” is the whole party: the jeweller, the two lovers, and the thieves taking them back to the river. sumayriyya, a kind of river boat; the print points its first two letters (السُمَيرية), and those marks are its own. ilā an, “until”; the print spells ilā with ي (الي) both times.

sentences.t: فَأَطْلَعُونَا فِيهَا وَإِذَا هِيَ الَّتِي عَدَّيْنَا فِيهَا بِالْأَمْسِ
sentences.tr: fa-aṭlaʿūnā fīhā wa-idhā hiya allatī ʿaddaynā fīhā bi-al-amsi
sentences.l: And they-made-us-go-up into-it, and behold, it (was) the-one we-crossed in-it yesterday.
sentences.i: They put us aboard, and lo, it was the very boat we had crossed in the day before.
sentences.n: The “we” is the jeweller with the two lovers; the thieves are “they”. “The one we crossed in yesterday” fits the lovers, whom the thieves carried over the river the night before, better than the jeweller, who crossed earlier that same night in a skiff (zawraq); he tells it here in the name of all three. aṭlaʿa (Form IV), “to make go up”, here “to put aboard”. ʿaddā (Form II), “to cross (a river)”, an everyday word for a crossing. wa-idhā, “and behold”, introduces a discovery.

sentences.t: فَقَذَفَ بِنَا الْمَلَّاحُ حَتَّى أَوْصَلَنَا إِلَى الْبَرِّ الثَّانِى فَأَنْزَلُونَا عَلَى جَانِبِ الْبَرِّ
sentences.tr: fa-qadhafa binā al-mallāḥu ḥattā awṣalanā ilā al-barri al-thānī fa-anzalūnā ʿalā jānibi al-barri
sentences.l: And the boatman rowed with-us until he-brought-us to the other bank (lit. the second land), and they-made-us-go-down on the side of the land.
sentences.i: The boatman rowed us across until he brought us to the far bank, and they set us down at the water's edge.
sentences.n: qadhafa bi-, literally “to throw with”, is used of rowing a boat (the miqdhāf is an oar): the bi- marks what is carried along. al-barr, “dry land”, here a river bank; al-barr al-thānī, “the second bank”, the far side. The print spells al-thānī with alif maqṣūra (ى), its frequent habit.

sentences.t: فَمَا اسْتَقَرَّ بِنَا الْجُلُوسُ عَلَى جَانِبِ الْبَرِّ وَمَا اسْتَرَحْنَا إِلَّا وَالْخَيَّالَةُ قَدْ أَحَاطُوا بِنَا مِثْلَ الْعِقْبَانِ مِنْ كُلِّ جَانِبٍ وَمَكَانٍ
sentences.tr: fa-mā istaqarra binā al-julūsu ʿalā jānibi al-barri wa-mā istaraḥnā illā wa-al-khayyālatu qad aḥāṭū binā mithla al-ʿiqbāni min kulli jānibin wa-makānin
sentences.l: And the sitting had-not settled with-us on the side of the land, and we-had-not rested, except that the horsemen had surrounded us like the eagles from every side and place.
sentences.i: We had hardly sat down on the bank, and had not yet caught our breath, when horsemen swooped down and surrounded us like eagles from every side.
sentences.n: mā … illā wa-, “not … but that (already)”: the two things happen at once, a favourite way of saying “no sooner … than”. al-khayyāla, “the horse-troop, horsemen”, a collective noun that takes a plural verb here (aḥāṭū) and a singular one below (qāla). aḥāṭa bi-, “to surround”, takes its object through bi-. ʿiqbān, plural of ʿuqāb, “eagle”. min kulli jānibin wa-makānin, “from every side and place”, a rhyming stock phrase.

sentences.t: فَوَثَبَ الَّذِينَ كَانُوا مَعَنَا عَاجِلًا كَالْعُقَابِ فَرَجَعَتْ لَهُمُ السُّمَيْرِيَّةُ فَنَزَلُوا فِيهَا وَدَفَعَ بِهِمُ الْمَلَّاحُ فَصَارُوا فِي وَسْطِ الْبَحْرِ وَذَهَبُوا
sentences.tr: fa-wathaba alladhīna kānū maʿanā ʿājilan ka-al-ʿuqābi fa-rajaʿat lahumu al-sumayriyyatu fa-nazalū fīhā wa-dafaʿa bihimu al-mallāḥu fa-ṣārū fī wasṭi al-baḥri wa-dhahabū
sentences.l: And those who were with-us leapt quickly like-the-eagle, and the boat came-back for-them, and they-went-down into-it, and the boatman pushed-off with-them, and they-became in the middle of the river, and they-went.
sentences.i: The men who had been with us sprang up swift as an eagle; the boat came back for them, they jumped in, the boatman pushed off, and in a moment they were out in midstream and away.
sentences.n: wathaba, a singular verb before its plural subject (alladhīna kānū maʿanā, the thieves), as Classical Arabic requires when the verb comes first. al-sumayriyya, a light river boat of the Tigris; the print's marks on السُمَيريّة are its own. al-baḥr, properly “sea”, is used throughout the Nights of a great river, here the Tigris. dafaʿa bi-, “to push off with (them)”; nazala fī, literally “to go down into”, to board a boat.

sentences.t: وَبَقِينَا نَحْنُ عَلَى الْبَرِّ عَلَى شَاطِئِ الْبَحْرِ لَا نَسْتَطِيعُ الْحَرَكَةَ وَلَا السُّكُونَ
sentences.tr: wa-baqīnā naḥnu ʿalā al-barri ʿalā shāṭiʾi al-baḥri lā nastaṭīʿu al-ḥarakata wa-lā al-sukūna
sentences.l: And we remained, we, on the land, on the shore of the river, not able (for) the moving nor the being-still.
sentences.i: And we were left on the bank, at the river's edge, unable either to move or to keep still.
sentences.n: lā nastaṭīʿu al-ḥarakata wa-lā al-sukūna, “we could neither move nor keep still”: the stock pair ḥaraka / sukūn, motion and rest, for helpless terror. The hamza of شاطئ is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَنَا الْخَيَّالَةُ مِنْ أَيْنَ أَنْتُمْ فَتَحَيَّرْنَا فِى الْجَوَابِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lanā al-khayyālatu min ayna antum fa-taḥayyarnā fī al-jawābi
sentences.l: And the horsemen said to-us: From where (are) you? And we-were-bewildered in the answer.
sentences.i: The horsemen asked us, “Where are you from?” and we did not know how to answer.
sentences.n: qāla, singular, with the collective al-khayyāla as subject (compare aḥāṭū above).

sentences.t: قَالَ الْجَوْهَرِيُّ فَقُلْتُ لَهُمْ إِنَّ هَؤُلَاءِ الَّذِينَ رَأَيْتُمُوهُمْ مَعَنَا كَانُوا عَيَّارِينَ لَانَعْرِفُهُمْ
sentences.tr: qāla al-jawhariyyu fa-qultu lahum inna hāʾulāʾi alladhīna raʾaytumūhum maʿanā kānū ʿayyārīna lā naʿrifuhum
sentences.l: The jeweller said: And I-said to-them: Those whom you-saw-them with-us were vagabonds we-do-not-know-them.
sentences.i: The jeweller said: I told them, “Those men you saw with us were rogues; we do not know them.
sentences.n: qāla al-jawharī, “the jeweller said”, is a signpost, not a change of speaker: the jeweller has been telling the story all along, and it reminds us whose “I” this is. ʿayyār, plural ʿayyārūn, a vagabond, sharper or gang-member, a stock figure of the urban underworld in the Nights. raʾaytumūhum: before an object suffix, the -tum of “you (pl.)” takes a linking -ū-. The print runs lā and naʿrifuhum together (لانعرفهم). The hamzas of هؤلاء and رأيتموهم are the print's own.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا نَحْنُ فَمُغَنُّونَ وَأَرَادُوا أَخْذَنَا لِنُغَنِّيَ لَهُمْ فَمَا تَخَلَّصْنَا مِنْهُمْ إِلَّا بِاللَّطَافَةِ وَلِينِ الْكَلَامِ
sentences.tr: wa-ammā naḥnu fa-mughannūna wa-arādū akhdhanā li-nughanniya lahum fa-mā takhallaṣnā minhum illā bi-al-laṭāfati wa-līni al-kalāmi
sentences.l: And as-for us, (we are) singers; and they-wanted our-taking so-that we-sing for-them; and we-did-not get-free from-them except by the gentleness and softness of the speech.
sentences.i: As for us, we are singers. They wanted to carry us off to sing for them, and we only got free of them by courtesy and soft words.
sentences.n: ammā … fa-, “as for … (then)”: the fa- opens the predicate, fa-mughannūna, “(we are) singers”. li-nughanniya, li- “in order to” with the subjunctive. The marks on لنغنّي and الّا are the print's own. The jeweller's tale is a ready lie: singers were hired and carried about by night, and could plausibly have fallen among such men.

sentences.t: فَأَفْرَجُوا عَنَّا فِى هَذِهِ السَّاعَةِ وَقَدْ كَانَ مِنْهُمْ مَا رَأَيْتُمْ مِنْ أَمْرِهِمْ
sentences.tr: fa-afrajū ʿannā fī hādhihi al-sāʿati wa-qad kāna minhum mā raʾaytum min amrihim
sentences.l: And they-released (from) us in this hour, and there-was from-them what you-saw of their-affair.
sentences.i: They let us go only this very hour, and what they did next you saw for yourselves.”
sentences.n: afraja ʿan, “to release, set free”, the person freed taking ʿan. kāna minhum mā raʾaytum, “there came from them what you saw”: their flight in the boat. The hamza of رأيتم is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَنَظَرَ الْخَيَّالَةُ إِلَى شَمْسِ النَّهَارِ وَعَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ وَقَالُوا لِي لَسْتَ صَادِقًا فِي كَلَامِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-naẓara al-khayyālatu ilā Shamsi al-Nahāri wa-ʿAliyyi ibni Bakkārin wa-qālū lī lasta ṣādiqan fī kalāmika
sentences.l: And the horsemen looked at Shams al-Nahār and ʿAlī son of Bakkār, and they-said to-me: You-are-not truthful in your-speech.
sentences.i: The horsemen looked at Shams al-Nahār and ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and said to me, “You are not telling the truth.
sentences.n: The collective al-khayyāla again takes first a singular verb (naẓara) and then a plural (qālū). laysa, “not to be”, takes its predicate in the accusative: lasta ṣādiqan. Their looks gave the lie away: these were plainly no hired singers.

sentences.t: فَإِنْ كُنْتَ صَادِقًا فَأَخْبِرْنَا مَنْ أَنْتُمْ وَمِنْ أَيْنَ أَنْتُمْ وَمَا مَوْضِعُكُمْ وَفِى أَيِّ الْحَارَٰتِ أَنْتُمْ سَاكِنُونَ
sentences.tr: fa-in kunta ṣādiqan fa-akhbirnā man antum wa-min ayna antum wa-mā mawḍiʿukum wa-fī ayyi al-ḥārāti antum sākinūna
sentences.l: So if you-are truthful, then inform-us who you (are), and from where you (are), and what (is) your-place, and in which of the quarters you (are) dwelling.
sentences.i: If you are, then tell us who you are and where you come from, where you live, and in which quarter of the city you make your home.”
sentences.n: The print has الحارت, which is best taken as al-ḥārāt, “the quarters” (plural of ḥāra, a city quarter), with the long ā before the t left unwritten; the letters are kept and the missing ā is shown by a small (dagger) alif. A misprint for الحارات is possible, but defective spellings of this kind occur in the print. The shadda of ايّ is the print's own.

sentences.t: قَالَ الْجَوْهَرِيُّ فَلَمْ أَدْرِمَا أَقُولُ لَهُمْ
sentences.tr: qāla al-jawhariyyu fa-lam adri mā aqūlu lahum
sentences.l: The jeweller said: And I-did-not know what I-should-say to-them.
sentences.i: The jeweller said: I did not know what to tell them.
sentences.n: lam adri, “I did not know”: after lam the verb is jussive, and darā loses its final long vowel (adrī → adri). The print runs it together with mā (ادرما).

sentences.t: فَوَثَبَتْ شَمْسُ النَّهَارِ وَتَقَدَّمَتْ إِلَى مُقَدَّمِ الْخَيَّالَةِ وَتَحَدَّثَتْ مَعَهُ سِرًّا
sentences.tr: fa-wathabat Shamsu al-Nahāri wa-taqaddamat ilā muqaddami al-khayyālati wa-taḥaddathat maʿahu sirran
sentences.l: And Shams al-Nahār leapt-up and went-forward to the leader of the horsemen and talked with-him secretly.
sentences.i: Then Shams al-Nahār sprang up, went over to the captain of the horsemen, and spoke with him privately.
sentences.n: muqaddam, “one put in front”, the leader or captain of a troop. What she told him is left unsaid; the reader can guess that she named her rank in the Caliph's household. The shadda of سرّا is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَنَزَلَ مِنْ فَوْقِ جَوَادِهِ وَأَرْكَبَهَا عَلَيْهِ وَأَخَذَ بِزِمَامِهَا وَصَارَ يَقُودُهَا
sentences.tr: fa-nazala min fawqi jawādihi wa-arkabahā ʿalayhi wa-akhadha bi-zimāmihā wa-ṣāra yaqūduhā
sentences.l: And he-got-down from on-top-of his-horse, and made-her-ride on-it, and took hold of her-halter, and began leading-her.
sentences.i: At once he got down from his horse, mounted her on it, took the bridle, and walked along leading her.
sentences.n: arkaba (Form IV), “to make ride, mount (someone) on”. akhadha bi-, “to take hold of”: the bi- marks the thing grasped. zimāmuhā, literally “her halter”: the halter of the horse she now rides, the rider standing for her mount. ṣāra with an imperfect, “began to (do)”. Leading a lady's horse on foot is a mark of deference.

sentences.t: وَكَذَلِكَ فَعَلَ آخَرُ بِالْفَتَى عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ وَفَعَلَ بِي أَيْضًا
sentences.tr: wa-ka-dhālika faʿala ākharu bi-al-fatā ʿAliyyi ibni Bakkārin wa-faʿala bī ayḍan
sentences.l: And likewise did another with the young-man ʿAlī son of Bakkār, and he-did (so) with-me too.
sentences.i: Another did the same for the young ʿAlī ibn Bakkār, and one did it for me as well.
sentences.n: faʿala bi-, “to do (something) to/with someone”. In faʿala bī the subject is unspoken: “(one) did so with me”. The madda of آخر is the print's own.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ مُقَدَّمَ الْخَيَّالَةِ لَمْ يَزَلْ سَائِرًا بِنَا إِلَى مَوْضِعٍ عَلَى جَانِبِ الْبَحْرِ وَصَاحَ بِالرَّطَانَةِ فَأَقْبَلَ لَهُ جَمَاعَةٌ مِنَ الْبَرِّيَّةِ مَعَهُمْ سُمَيْرِيَّتَانِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna muqaddama al-khayyālati lam yazal sāʾiran binā ilā mawḍiʿin ʿalā jānibi al-baḥri wa-ṣāḥa bi-al-raṭānati fa-aqbala lahu jamāʿatun mina al-barriyyati maʿahum sumayriyyatāni
sentences.l: Then the leader of the horsemen did-not cease going with-us to a place on the side of the river, and he-shouted in the foreign-tongue, and there-came to-him a company from the open-land, with-them two-boats.
sentences.i: The captain of the horsemen kept on with us until we came to a spot on the riverbank. There he called out in a foreign tongue, and a band of men came up from the land with two boats.
sentences.n: thumma inna, “then (it was that)”, a narrative opener that puts the following noun in the accusative (muqaddama). lam yazal, “did not cease”, with a participle: “kept on going”. sāra bi-, “to go with, take along”: sāʾiran binā, “taking us along”. raṭāna is speech in a foreign or unintelligible tongue (Lane); here perhaps a call in Persian or Turkish, or a watchword the boatmen would know. min al-barriyya is read “from the open land”, i.e. from the landward side; one could also read al-bariyya, “people, creatures” (“a number of folk”). sumayriyyatāni, dual of sumayriyya, “two boats”.

sentences.t: فَطَلَّعَنَا الْمُقَدَّمُ فِى وَاحِدَةٍ وَهُوَ مَعَنَا وَطَلَعَ أَصْحَابُهُ فِي الثَّانِيَةِ وَقَذَفُوا بِنَا إِلَى أَنِ انْتَهَيْنَا إِلَى دَارِ الْخِلَافَةِ وَنَحْنُ نُكَابِدُ الْمَوْتَ مِنْ شِدَّةِ الْخَوْفِ
sentences.tr: fa-ṭallaʿanā al-muqaddamu fī wāḥidatin wa-huwa maʿanā wa-ṭalaʿa aṣḥābuhu fī al-thāniyati wa-qadhafū binā ilā an intahaynā ilā dāri al-khilāfati wa-naḥnu nukābidu al-mawta min shiddati al-khawfi
sentences.l: And the leader made-us-go-up into one, and he (was) with-us, and his-companions went-up into the second; and they-rowed with-us until we-reached the House of the Caliphate, and we (were) suffering death from the intensity of the fear.
sentences.i: The captain put us into one of them and came aboard with us, while his men took the other; and they rowed us on until we reached the Caliph's palace, all the while dying a thousand deaths for fear.
sentences.n: ṭallaʿa (Form II), “to make go up”, here “to put aboard”, a colloquial causative beside the Form IV aṭlaʿa used above; the print's fatḥa on the lām (فطلَعنا) fits either ṭallaʿanā, “he put us aboard”, read here because al-muqaddamu is its subject, or ṭalaʿnā, “we went aboard”, which would leave al-muqaddam hanging. ṭalaʿa fī, “to go up into”, to board. ilā an, “until”. dār al-khilāfa, “the abode of the Caliphate”, the Caliph's palace, past which the river route ran. kābada, “to endure, suffer (hardship)”.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ نَزَلْ سَائِرِينَ إِلَى أَنِ انْتَهَيْنَا إِلَى الْمَحَلِّ الَّذِي نَتَوَصَّلُ مِنْهُ إِلَى مَوْضِعِنَا
sentences.tr: wa-lam nazal sāʾirīna ilā an intahaynā ilā al-maḥalli alladhī natawaṣṣalu minhu ilā mawḍiʿinā
sentences.l: And we-did-not cease going until we-reached the spot which we-get through-from-it to our-place.
sentences.i: On we went until we came to the landing from which one reaches our house.
sentences.n: tawaṣṣala ilā (Form V), “to make one's way to, reach”: natawaṣṣalu minhu ilā mawḍiʿinā, “from which we get to our place”. maḥall, “place, spot”, here the landing-place.

sentences.t: فَنَزَلْنَا عَلَى الْبَرِّ وَمَشَيْنَا وَمَعَنَا جَمَاعَةٌ مِنَ الْخَيَّالَةِ يُؤَانِسُونَنَا إِلَى أَنْ دَخَلْنَا الدَّارَ
sentences.tr: fa-nazalnā ʿalā al-barri wa-mashaynā wa-maʿanā jamāʿatun mina al-khayyālati yuʾānisūnanā ilā an dakhalnā al-dāra
sentences.l: And we-got-down onto the land and walked, and with-us a company of the horsemen keeping-us-company, until we-entered the house.
sentences.i: We went ashore and walked on, with a party of the horsemen keeping us company, until we were inside the house.
sentences.n: ānasa (Form III), “to keep company with, cheer by one's company”: yuʾānisūnanā, “keeping us company”, a circumstantial clause. The hamza of يؤانسوننا is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَحِينَ دَخَلْنَاهَا وَدَّعَنَا مَنْ كَانَ مَعَنَا مِنَ الْخَيَّالَةِ وَ مَضَوْا إِلَى حَالِ سَبِيلِهِمْ
sentences.tr: wa-ḥīna dakhalnāhā waddaʿanā man kāna maʿanā mina al-khayyālati wa-maḍaw ilā ḥāli sabīlihim
sentences.l: And when we-entered-it, those-who were with-us of the horsemen bade-us-farewell, and went to the state of their-way.
sentences.i: As soon as we had gone in, the horsemen who had come with us took their leave and went their way.
sentences.n: ḥīna, “at the time when”. waddaʿa (Form II), “to bid farewell”. maḍā ilā ḥāli sabīlihi, literally “went to the state of his road”, “went about his business”, a stock phrase of the Nights. The print sets the wa- of wa-maḍaw at the end of a line, apart from its verb; it is kept as printed.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا نَحْنُ فَقَدْ دَخَلْنَا مَكَانَنَا وَنَحْنُ لَانَقْدِرُ أَنْ نَتَحَرَّكَ مِنْ مَكَانِنَا وَلَانَدْرِي الصَّبَاحَ مِنَ الْمَسَاءِ
sentences.tr: wa-ammā naḥnu fa-qad dakhalnā makānanā wa-naḥnu lā naqdiru an nataḥarraka min makāninā wa-lā nadrī al-ṣabāḥa mina al-masāʾi
sentences.l: And as-for us, we-had-entered our-place, and we (were) not able to move from our-place, and not knowing the morning from the evening.
sentences.i: As for us, we went into our quarters, unable to stir from where we lay, not knowing morning from evening.
sentences.n: ammā … fa-qad, “as for … (then)”. The print runs lā together with the following verb twice (لانقدر, لاندري). lā nadrī al-ṣabāḥa mina al-masāʾi, “we did not know morning from evening”, i.e. we lost all sense of time.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ نَزَلْ عَلَى هَذِهِ الْحَالَةِ إِلَى أَنْ أَصْبَحَ الصَّبَاحُ
sentences.tr: wa-lam nazal ʿalā hādhihi al-ḥālati ilā an aṣbaḥa al-ṣabāḥu
sentences.l: And we-did-not cease (being) in this condition until the morning morninged.
sentences.i: So we remained until morning came.
sentences.n: aṣbaḥa al-ṣabāḥu, “the morning dawned”, a figura etymologica: verb and subject from the same root.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا جَاءَ آخِرُ النَّهَارِ سَقَطَ عَلِيُّ بْنُ بَكَّارٍ مَغْشِيًّا عَلَيْهِ وَبَكَى عَلَيْهِ النِّسَاءُ وَالرِّجَالُ وَهُوَ مَطْرُوحٌ لَمْ يَتَحَرَّكْ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā jāʾa ākhiru al-nahāri saqaṭa ʿAliyyu ibnu Bakkārin maghshiyyan ʿalayhi wa-bakā ʿalayhi al-nisāʾu wa-al-rijālu wa-huwa maṭrūḥun lam yataḥarrak
sentences.l: And when the end of the day came, ʿAlī son of Bakkār fell fainted-upon, and the women and the men wept over-him, and he (was) thrown-down, he-did-not move.
sentences.i: When evening came, ʿAlī ibn Bakkār fell down in a faint, and the women and men of the house wept over him as he lay stretched out without a movement.
sentences.n: maghshiyyan ʿalayhi, “fainted” (literally “covered over”, as by a swoon), a passive participle that keeps its preposition. bakā, singular, before a plural subject (al-nisāʾ wa-al-rijāl). bakā ʿalā, “to weep over”. lam yataḥarrak, “he did not move”, jussive after lam. The hamza of جاء and the madda of آخر are the print's own.

sentences.t: فَجَاؤُنِي بَعْضُ أَهْلِهِ وَأَيْقَظُونِي وَقَالُوا حَدِّثْنَا بِمَاجَرَى عَلَى وَالِدِنَا وَمَا هَذَا الْحَالُ الَّذِي هُوَ فِيهِ فَقُلْتُ لَهُمْ يَا قَوْمُ اسْمَعُوا كَلَامِي
sentences.tr: fa-jāʾūnī baʿḍu ahlihi wa-ayqaẓūnī wa-qālū ḥaddithnā bi-mā jarā ʿalā wālidinā wa-mā hādhā al-ḥālu alladhī huwa fīhi fa-qultu lahum yā qawmu ismaʿū kalāmī
sentences.l: And there-came-to-me some of his-family, and they-woke-me, and they-said: Tell-us of-what happened to our-father, and what (is) this state which he (is) in-it? And I-said to-them: O people, hear my-speech.
sentences.i: Then some of his family came to me and woke me, and said, “Tell us what has befallen our father, and what this state is that he is in.” I said to them, “Good people, hear what I have to say.”
sentences.n: jāʾūnī, “they came to me”, is spelt جاوني, without the hamza; it is supplied above the wāw. The verb is plural with the singular baʿḍ, by sense (“some” are several people). ḥaddatha bi-, “to tell (someone) of”: the matter told takes bi-. The print runs bi-mā and jarā together (بماجرى). wālidinā, “our father”, is odd from ʿAlī's household, since ʿAlī is a young man; perhaps “our master” is meant, or his household speak loosely; the word is kept as printed. al-ḥāl is masculine here (hādhā al-ḥālu) beside the feminine al-ḥāla above; both are found. yā qawmu, “O people”, “Good folk”. The jeweller, it seems, had spent the night in ʿAlī's house.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَ زَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she-fell-silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The object comes before the subject: Shahrazāda is the one overtaken, al-ṣabāḥu the morning that overtakes. The print splits the name in two (شهر زاد). al-kalām al-mubāḥ, “the permitted speech”, the talk allowed her until dawn; the rhyme ṣabāḥ / mubāḥ closes every night.
